item.title: 🔴 Node2Shell puts Microsoft and Node.js on Brotli patch duty
item.description:
Why this matters: Remote-code-execution risk — assess exposure and patch or mitigate quickly.

A vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression library could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code in applications that use an affected Brotli decoder to process compressed data.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the high-severity flaw was first flagged in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The issue stems from an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt process memory, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or denial of service (DoS).

The Node.js project disclosed the vulnerability on October 21, 2026, alongside security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. The exposure, however, extended beyond Node.js, forcing Microsoft to release out-of-band security updates for.NET on October 25 to address the same CVE in its Brotli decompression implementation.

Separate research published by OpenSourceMalware identified the vulnerable decoder code in the Python packages Brotli and brotlicffi. Both packages…

An Alibaba AI model generated an unexpected command to upload data to a Beijing-region cloud storage service during a cybersecurity evaluation, rival developer Cohere said, raising concerns about the security of AI agents with access to enterprise systems.

The model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, was being tested using Microsoft’s CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark, which tasked it with writing a rule to detect malicious file downloads followed by execution. Instead, it inspected local files and system settings before generating the unexpected command, according to Cohere’s report.

The Canadian AI company said its isolated testing environment blocked the outgoing request. The model had indicated in its generated reasoning that it would not use any tools, contradicting the command it subsequently generated.

item.title: 🔵 ‘Citizen AI’ can help IT leaders spark business solutions — if done right
item.description:

AI fluency has long mattered to Sambit Dutta. When he joined global chemical manufacturer Hexion this year as SVP of AI transformation, his strategy included bringing “AI to the masses, where the people can not only just consume AI, but also become what we call builders.”

Dutta has made citizen AI a cornerstone of Hexion’s IT strategy because he believes that when the creativity and domain expertise of employees is centralized and funneled through a business analyst or developer, “there are always things lost in translation.” Further, “there’s a queuing process where that request ultimately gets queued, and then based on dollars and other priorities, never gets executed,” he adds.

Dutta also believes that innovation unleashed at the grassroots level is how enterprises achieve true transformation. And it facilitates change management because people become more receptive to absorbing technology at that level, he says.

“We firmly believe that we are at a stage where citizen development has finally taken off” at Hexion, Dutton says.

item.title: 🔵 AI and hybrid work are rewriting the rules of persona-based provisioning
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

AI and the rise of hybrid work are rewriting the rules of persona-based provisioning. Equipping the workforce by persona used to be a straightforward exercise: the org chart supplied the groups, a stereotype supplied the requirements, and the model held because most people worked roughly the same way. Not anymore. AI keeps redrawing what roles need, and hybrid work has scattered where they need it. Together, they’ve changed the inputs persona building runs on.

The inputs changed; the principle didn’t. Sorting employees into representative types and equipping each accordingly is still how smart device fleets get provisioned. But the old build — a role, a department, a rough sketch — was drawn from a workplace that no longer exists. The new build starts from the work: where it happens, what it demands, what it costs when it stops.

item.title: 🔵 Modern work needs modern device management
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Device management does not often surface in executive conversations. But it probably should.

The hardware employees use every day has quietly become one of the most consequential investments an organization makes—shaping how productively people work, how securely the business operates, how cleanly it meets compliance obligations, and how prepared it is for the next wave of AI-driven work. In practice, when they work well, the business runs quietly. When they don’t, performance slows, call quality suffers, productivity takes a hit, and avoidable IT tickets pile up.

That makes the employee device experience a leadership issue, not just an IT one. The downstream effects touch retention, output, support cost, and how employees feel about the organization that equips them. item.title: 🟠 The metric that makes your IT org look healthier than it is
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

An executive IT dashboard can stay green for a year while the risks it is supposed to surface keep growing. Availability above target every month. Service levels met. Patch compliance climbing quarter over quarter. Every number accurate, and every one trusted by the executive team.

When trouble finally arrives, it skips amber entirely. It comes as an outage, an audit finding or a security incident, and the first question in the room is why the dashboard said everything was fine.

In my work with technology leaders and executive teams, I have learned that a dashboard can be technically accurate and still leave leadership dangerously misinformed. Usually nobody fudged anything. The numbers were built to summarize, and a summary is very good at hiding the one thing an executive most needs to see. Three metrics produce most of that false comfort at the executive level. I would not put any of them in front of a CEO or a board as a headline number.

Cybercriminals don’t need AI to compromise an organization, but AI is making its way into classic attack methods and changing how quickly such attacks can progress. Tasks that once required attackers to manually sift through information and piece together how an organization operates can be accelerated by AI, reducing the time defenders have to detect and intervene.

A recent example of this is EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service platform that helps attackers gain access to Microsoft 365 inboxes and then uses AI to analyze the environment to determine the most effective next steps. First identified in February 2026, EvilTokens exploits the device authorization grant flow of OAuth 2.0 to gain access to Microsoft accounts without having to create fraudulent login pages. item.title: 🟠 Your senior engineers need junior questions more than juniors need answers
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

When juniors take naive questions to an AI assistant instead of a colleague, dashboards record fewer interruptions and higher velocity. What they miss is the erosion of senior engineers’ architectural fluency, and the single point of failure that hardens until an outage forces someone to explain the system out loud.

Over the past year, I watched engineering teams celebrate a quiet drop in Slack interruptions. item.title: 🟠 Dual BIOS: The laptop security feature SMBs don’t know they need
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Every security checklist starts with the basics: strong passwords, multifactor authentication, spotting phishing, and keeping software up to date. All four protect what happens after a laptop starts. But some attackers are more focused on what happens before.

That’s the domain of the BIOS, the first code that runs when a laptop powers on. It checks the hardware, then hands control to the operating system. Malware planted at this level can load before the operating system does, so it can evade antivirus tools and even survive a drive wipe or reinstall. 

For small and midsize businesses (SMBs), the cost of an incident goes beyond the bill to fix it.  It’s also about the work that stops in the meantime. The Verizon Business 2026 Breach Impact Study (which analyzes cyber insurance claims), found that SMBs suffered losses accounting for up to 7% of their total revenue. It also identified business interruption as the fastest growing source of loss.

item.title: 🔴 Stop the insider threat lurking in AI agents
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

The insider threat model rests on a simple premise: legitimate access to business systems is used in ways you didn’t intend. When an employee is onboarded, there is typically an access review, a background check, and least-privilege provisioning. Trust is extended, and occasionally that trust can create risk to business systems and data.

This process does not apply to AI agents. Across enterprises deploying AI, powerful endpoint agents that execute code, call tools, access credentials, move data, and make autonomous decisions are running with full user-level permissions. Many weren’t reviewed by IT, security, or legal. They were deployed by an employee who clicked “install” and have been operating with that employee’s level of access.

item.title: 🔴 China-linked hackers used agentic AI in attack on 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used an open-source agentic AI framework to turn its stolen credentials against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft said.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence attributed the activity to Storm-0940, which it said has used the ARTEX framework since as early as September 2026 to automate attacks on hundreds of organizations. In some cases, the group gained privileged cloud access less than three hours after first targeting a victim. Microsoft said the activity did not result from a compromise of or vulnerability in its own systems, products, or services.

“This activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and allows them to scale their operations exponentially,” Microsoft said in a blog post.
